name: Creative Studio
title: Building an ad creation and editing experience
intro: I led the full-stack build of Creative Studio, which lets marketers create AI-generated ads and revise them for new messages and formats without starting over.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: My role covered product, design, frontend, backend, ML, and agentic systems. I worked with product and design to test workflows and the ML team to test model outputs, while owning the technical direction and contributing code through launch.

keyDecisions: Keep creation and revision in one workflow so marketers can adapt an ad without starting over.
Use customer feedback and quick prototypes for bigger product changes; ship smaller iterations fast and measure what happens.
Design the frontend, backend, async messaging, and AI agents as one system that preserves context and shows progress.

sections.title: Start with the marketer's real task
sections.body: We treated creation and revision as the same job. A marketer could adapt an ad for a new message or format without losing the visual choices that made it part of the same campaign. Each revision kept the existing context instead of sending the user back to a blank canvas.

sections.title: Shape the workflow through feedback
sections.body: Customer feedback did not stop at a product brief. I worked with our product manager and designers to decide what should change, then built those changes into the interface. We tuned the path from a first draft to specific edits in the message, visual direction, and aspect ratio.

sections.title: Connect the experience to agentic systems
sections.body: The interface depended on the frontend, backend, async messaging, and AI/ML agents working as one product. I defined how those pieces exchanged state so users could see progress, keep their editing context, and understand where each generated result came from.

sections.title: Own the path to production
sections.body: I stayed hands-on in product design, interaction design, architecture, implementation, and launch. With fewer handoffs, customer feedback could turn into working software without the original intent getting diluted along the way.

name: Marketplace discovery & checkout
title: Helping people find benefits that fit
intro: Employees use Fringe points to buy products and services. I redesigned and rebuilt marketplace discovery and checkout so users could get from a relevant recommendation to checkout with fewer steps.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: I worked with product and design to improve how people found and bought benefits in the Fringe marketplace. My work spanned user research, prototyping, interaction design, experimentation, and production engineering, carrying ideas from early exploration through shipped experiences and measurable product outcomes.

keyDecisions: Start with user tests and analytics instead of assumptions.
Use prototypes and A/B tests to discard weak ideas before spending time building them.
Keep iterating after launch, using production data to improve recommendations, repeat purchases, and the cart.

steps.title: Discover interest-based categories
steps.description: Browse recommended vendors by what matters to you.

steps.title: Add to cart
steps.description: Move from browsing to checkout with fewer steps.

steps.title: Complete the purchase
steps.description: Checkout with fewer steps and higher confidence.

sections.title: Find the friction before choosing a solution
sections.body: I worked with design and product to run user tests and guided interviews. We learned what people came to the marketplace to find, where they got stuck, and how the cart contributed to the problem. We prototyped alternatives and ran A/B tests rather than assuming the first design was right.

sections.title: Design for relevance and repeat behavior
sections.body: We grouped recommendations around users' interests instead of showing everyone the same undifferentiated marketplace. Favorites and recurring purchases made it easier to return to products people already valued. A shorter checkout path and clearer cart removed decisions that were getting in the way.

sections.title: Measure the journey in production
sections.body: Production analytics showed an approximately 30% reduction in time from marketplace discovery to add-to-cart. The redesigned cart also increased completed checkouts. We did not call the work finished at launch; we kept measuring how people actually used it.

sections.title: Build a foundation for faster experiments
sections.body: To keep each experiment from becoming a one-off, I led the frontend architecture behind the product. We aligned a shared component library across Figma and Storybook, moved from JavaScript to TypeScript, Create React App to Vite, styled-components to Tailwind CSS, and upgraded React from 16 through 18. Development time dropped by approximately 40%, and later experiments were faster to build.

name: ADP Thrive
title: A purchase without another account
intro: ADP Thrive gave Fringe a new place to sell its benefits. I defined the MVP, designed the experience, and led UI development through launch and support.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: I helped define the MVP, designed the product, and led the frontend implementation through launch. I worked with product, design, and engineering to resolve UX and technical constraints so people could buy benefits without creating a separate Fringe account.

keyDecisions: Let people buy Fringe offerings without creating a separate Fringe account.
Make the marketplace feel native to Thrive but authentically Fringe.
Make it fast. Building a tiny new app with auto-auth, Fringe APIs, and Stripe is better than extending the existing Fringe platform.

steps.title: Discover and select
steps.description: Discover exclusive offerings and Fringe benefits where users already shop.

steps.title: Buyers stay put
steps.description: View and purchase offerings in an officially-branded Fringe experience. No separate Fringe account or external redirect required.

steps.title: Reach a new audience
steps.description: Purchases and exposure grew as Fringe reached people who may not have discovered the platform otherwise.

sections.title: Choose the constraint that mattered
sections.body: The ADP marketplace put Fringe in front of a new audience. The catch was account creation. Asking every buyer to register with Fringe added friction before they could purchase anything, so I made removing that requirement the center of the MVP.

sections.title: Define and deliver the MVP
sections.body: I scoped the first release around one complete purchase journey, not a collection of disconnected screens. I designed the experience and led the UI development, so decisions about scope and interaction behavior went straight into the shipped product.

sections.title: Connect identity, commerce, and fulfillment
sections.body: A React and Vite frontend used OAuth and an authentication proxy to call Fringe REST APIs. Stripe handled payment and fulfillment. Buyers stayed inside the branded Thrive experience without creating or navigating through a separate Fringe account.

sections.title: Carry the product beyond launch
sections.body: I stayed with the product through launch and supported it afterward. The simpler buying flow gave Fringe another sales channel and reached people who may not have found its products otherwise.

name: Redesigning a $1.2B fintech pipeline
title: Redesigning a $1.2B fintech pipeline
intro: I led the product and interaction design for CapCenter's loan application, then built the frontend that put the redesign in customers' hands.

liveWork.label: Open the live loan application
liveWork.note: The interface has changed slightly since this work shipped, but the UX flow and UI architecture remain.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: I owned the product and interaction design and the frontend implementation. Working with business stakeholders, I turned lending and regulatory requirements into user flows that customers could understand without losing what the business needed.

keyDecisions: Use customer research and stakeholder interviews to find friction in the company's primary revenue journey.
Keep design and frontend development together so product decisions survive implementation.
Treat launch as the start of the feedback loop, not the end of the project.

steps.title: Product design
steps.description: Research the existing application, interview customers and stakeholders, and redesign the company's primary revenue stream.

steps.title: Frontend & product engineering
steps.description: Build the new interface and architecture, then capture feedback.

sections.title: The product context
sections.body: The loan application sat at the center of CapCenter's digital business for mortgage, lending, and real estate customers. It was also one of the projects where my product design and frontend engineering responsibilities were most tightly connected.

sections.title: The challenge
sections.body: The government's URLA form is a complex document that must be filled out accurately to avoid legal and financial risks. It also contains a lot of optional fields that can be confusing for borrowers. We needed an experience that was easy for borrowers to understand with rigorous enough validation to avoid legal and financial risks.

sections.title: What I owned
sections.body: I led the user research and redesign, then built the frontend. That made me responsible for both what the application should do and how it actually behaved in the browser.

sections.title: Results
sections.body: In its first year, the redesigned loan application pipeline grew over 500% to $1.2 billion in loan volume. The redesign alone raised CapCenter's Net Promoter Score (NPS) by 2+ points.

name: Loan Officer Assignment Tool
title: Matching clients with loan consultants
intro: I designed an internal tool that saved the company 750+ hours per year by assigning clients to loan consultants based on location, qualifications, and availability.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: I interviewed managers to find out why assigning clients took so long, then designed and built the tool that automated the work. I handled the interaction design and frontend implementation, including the controls managers used to review assignments and update consultant criteria.

keyDecisions: Find the repetitive assignment work that was costing managers the most time.
Turn location, qualifications, availability, and capacity into explicit matching rules.
Give managers one place to review assignments and update the rules behind future matches.

sections.title: Automate the assignment
sections.body: Managers were losing time in two places: finding the right consultant for each client and keeping consultant criteria and capacity current. I built a tool that matched clients using location, skills, qualifications, and availability. Managers could review the results and update the underlying rules in the same place.

sections.title: Give managers 125+ hours back
sections.body: After rollout, the tool saved each manager more than 30 minutes per day, or over 125 hours per year. I designed the interface in Figma and built it with React, Bootstrap, and TypeScript. We deployed it through Azure CI/CD.

name: Real Estate Property Search
title: From finding a home to booking a tour
intro: I designed and built CapCenter's home search, where buyers could find listings, browse photos, and schedule a tour without leaving the site.

liveWork.label: Open the live home search
liveWork.note: The interface has changed slightly since this work shipped, but the UX flow and UI architecture remain.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: I designed and built a home search that connected property discovery with lending and affordability. I shaped how people searched, compared financial tradeoffs, and moved between finding a home and deciding how to finance it, then built the frontend experience.

keyDecisions: Design the experience around the trip from finding a property to scheduling a tour.
Use MLS data and Elasticsearch for listings, with Google Maps for location.
Keep tour scheduling inside CapCenter instead of sending buyers to another marketplace.

sections.title: Connect discovery to the tour
sections.body: Most buyers would start on Zillow or Redfin, but CapCenter wanted a search product of its own. I designed the path from browsing listings and photos to scheduling a tour directly with CapCenter.

sections.title: Take the design into production
sections.body: I designed the experience in Figma and built the frontend with React, TypeScript, and Bootstrap. Elasticsearch and MLS databases powered the listings, while Google Maps APIs handled the map experience. We deployed it to Kubernetes through Azure CI/CD.

sections.title: Results
sections.body: After the property search launched, CapCenter saw an increase of more than 200% in tour leads.

name: NBA Top Shot / Dapper Labs
title: Personalizing NBA Top Shot messaging with collection data
intro: I worked with Dapper Labs' data engineering team to make NBA Top Shot collection data usable in automated, personalized email for more than two million users.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: I worked with growth, data, and engineering on onboarding, personalization, and experiments for NBA Top Shot. I built the data connections and automation that made targeted campaigns and A/B tests possible.

keyDecisions: Normalize collection data before sending it from internal systems to Customer.io and HubSpot.
Represent ownership at the individual collectible level so campaigns can respond to what a user actually owns.
Use clean collection data for onboarding experiments, A/B tests, and automated messages to more than two million users.

steps.label: Normalize and sync
steps.title: Prepare data for Customer.io and HubSpot

steps.label: Apply
steps.title: Support personalized email and onboarding experiments

sections.title: Connect data to the experience
sections.body: I worked with data engineering to sync internal databases with Customer.io and HubSpot. Before that data could drive personalized email, I normalized it into a shape the marketing tools could use reliably.

sections.title: Support onboarding and internal operations
sections.body: I supported onboarding campaigns and built internal communication tools with the Slack API and Google Apps Script.

sections.title: Target messages down to individual collectibles
sections.body: Once the collection data was clean, we could run A/B tests and automate messages based on the packs a user owned or an upcoming drop. We could target messages as narrowly as one collectible in a user's collection.

name: San Joaquin Matching Engine
title: Helping social workers find prospective adoptive families
intro: At Dito, I designed and built a tool that helped San Joaquin County social workers compare prospective adoptive families for children awaiting adoption. The matching engine used weighted criteria to rank potential matches for review.

facts.label: Project role
facts.value: Lead UX Designer & Lead UI Developer

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: I led the UX design and frontend development of a Section 508-compliant matching application. I interviewed stakeholders, prototyped the workflow, designed the interactions, and built the production interface around the county's operating requirements.

keyDecisions: Turn the county's matching criteria into weighted rankings without taking the final decision away from social workers.
Show ranked results beside family profiles so workers can see the information behind a potential match.
Meet Section 508 requirements and move the frontend to TypeScript so the application is easier to maintain.

steps.label: Select
steps.title: Start with a child's profile
steps.description: Choose the profile to compare against prospective families.

steps.label: Match
steps.title: Apply weighted criteria
steps.description: The engine scores and ranks potential matches.

steps.label: Review
steps.title: Inspect potential matches
steps.description: Social workers can open family profiles alongside the ranked results.

sections.title: Bring the comparison into one workflow
sections.body: The matching engine was part of the county's I-CAN initiative. Social workers compared a child's profile with prospective families using several criteria. We put ranked results and profile details in the same workflow so workers could see why a family appeared as a potential match.

sections.title: Design and build the interface
sections.body: I designed the workflow in Adobe XD and built the interface in Angular with Material Design. The UI met Section 508 accessibility requirements. We also moved the frontend from JavaScript to TypeScript and deployed it to Google App Engine through GitLab CI/CD.

sections.title: Project recognition
sections.body: The project received a 2017 Innovation Award from the California County Information Services Directors Association (CCISDA).
